source.title: RankMixer: Scaling Up Ranking Models in Industrial Recommenders
source.authors: Jie Zhu; Zhifang Fan; Xiaoxie Zhu; Yu-Chen Jiang; Hang-Yu Wang; Xin-Tian Han; Haoran Ding; Xinmin Wang; Wenlin Zhao; Zhen Gong; Hui Yang; Zheng Chai; Zhe Chen; Yu-Chao Zheng; Qi-Wei Chen; Feng Zhang; Xun Zhou; Peng Xu; Xiao Yang; Di Wu; Zuo-Tao Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figure 2's plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates scaling in industrial recommendation models, a different training/application setting from language-model pretraining, and reports scaling results using recommendation AUC rather than held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The relevant results concern recommendation-model AUC scaling with parameters and FLOPs. The paper does not measure language-model pretraining loss, report fitted power-law exponents, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its online engagement metrics and component ablations do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper for industrial recommendation ranking. Its scaling evidence is Figure 2, which plots finish-AUC gain against log params and log FLOPs for RankMixer and rival architectures. The text only says RankMixer shows 'the steepest scaling law' and is 'consistently superior'. It gives no power-law fit, no exponent, no loss curve, no extrapolation test and no compute-optimal allocation. The scaling result is used to rank the authors' own method against baselines, not to test whether a power-law form holds in recommendation. Table 1 compares the authors' method with others at about 100M parameters, plus one 1B point. So the paper relies on the scaling-law idea as motivation and reports its own method's performance (T4), not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that RankMixer, a hardware-aware token-mixing plus per-token-FFN architecture, outperforms prior feature-interaction models and shows the 'steepest scaling law' in AUC versus params and FLOPs. It raises MFU from 4.5% to 45% and allows a 70x parameter increase to 1B at similar latency. Deployed on Douyin, it raised active days by 0.3% and usage duration by 1.08%. The 'scaling directions give near-identical performance' point is a secondary observation within Section 4.3.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales an industrial recommendation architecture and evaluates recommendation AUC, not language models trained for held-out pretraining loss; it does not fit or report comparable language-model scaling-law exponents.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that increasing width, feature-token count, or depth yields almost identical performance at comparable scale; wider hidden dimensions produce larger matrix-multiply shapes and higher MFU than adding layers. No quantitative condition-specific scaling results are supplied for these comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: For RankMixer recommendation models, the authors state that scaling width D, tokens T or depth L gives 'almost identical performance', with quality tracking total parameters. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation ranking models, offline AUC depends mainly on dense parameter count, not on the scaling direction (depth, width or token count).

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 shows finish-AUC gain rising with log params and log FLOPs, with architecture-dependent slopes: RankMixer steepest, DHEN and MoE poor. Values are not given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The slope of recommendation-model AUC scaling depends strongly on the feature-interaction architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (2025)
record.problems: The evidence relevant to scaling consists of recommendation AUC rather than held-out loss. Figure 2's plotted values are unavailable in the supplied text, and the paper reports no fitted power-law exponents, fit uncertainty, or quantitative test of extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted. Online engagement and advertising metrics, architecture ablations, and serving-efficiency results were left out because they do not measure the scaling-law behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All: no compute-optimal parameter/data split is studied.
Language-model loss versus shape is not studied. Only a qualitative recommender-model statement is given (see fits_no_version).
Whether a power-law form holds for recommendation models: no fit, exponents or loss values are reported, and Figure 2 values are unavailable.

missing.what: Numeric values of the Figure 2 AUC-gain curves for each architecture, and any fitted form
Qualitative claim that width, depth and token scaling give near-identical AUC at equal parameter count, with no numbers

record.verdict_notes: I changed the reader's 'tests/T3' to 'uses_without_test/T4'. The scaling evidence is qualitative, on AUC, with no fitted form, and it serves to rank the authors' architecture against baselines. So it cannot bear out or contradict V5's power-law form, and the reader's limits_scope label on V5 is dropped. Online A/B and serving-cost results are not relevant to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.

The study examines scaling in industrial recommender models, but does not establish that the same fitted power-law form holds: it reports AUC trends rather than loss and supplies no fitted exponents or quantitative fit results.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

relation.reason: The study uses scaling expectations to design RankMixer and reports its performance, without testing the catalog's defined scaling-law claims.

tranche.reason: Scaling motivates the architecture, while the reported evidence compares recommendation performance and efficiency. It does not establish the power-law form required by V5 or test another defined claim version.

source_check.notes: Figure 2's plotted numerical values are unavailable in the supplied text; its caption specifies only a logarithmic x-axis. Section 4.3 also reports similar recommendation performance across scaling directions, but does not measure the loss named by V4.
